```{=html}
<header class="dg-head dg-head-section"><p class="dg-kicker">Chapter 9 <span class="dg-sep">•</span> <a href="index.html">Newton-Cartan Theory</a></p><h1 class="dg-title"><span class="dg-secnum">9.5</span> Gravity in the Connection</h1></header>
<ul class="dg-itemize dg-depth-1">
<li><p>With gravity, the observation changes. In a stratified chart <span class="math inline">\((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\)</span> with Cartesian spatial coordinates, non-rotating axes and origin at rest w.r.t. the sources, every freely falling body obeys <span class="math inline">\(\ddot{\gamma}^\alpha_\mathcal{U} = - \partial x_\alpha\left\lfloor \phi \right\rceil\)</span>, independently of its velocity and mass, where <span class="math inline">\(\phi \in C^\infty(\mathcal{U})\)</span> satisfies <span class="math inline">\(\Delta \phi \coloneqq \sum_{\alpha} \partial x_\alpha\left\lfloor \partial x_\alpha\left\lfloor \phi \right\rceil \right\rceil = 4 \pi G_N \rho\)</span>. Matching coefficients gives  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            \Gamma^\alpha_{00} = \partial x_\alpha\left\lfloor \phi \right\rceil,
            \qquad
            \text{all other } \Gamma^i_{jk} = 0
            \longrightarrow
            m \, \ddot{\gamma}^\alpha_\mathcal{U}(t)
            = - m \, \partial_\alpha \left[ \phi \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \right] \big( \mathscr{X}(\gamma(t)) \big),
        \end{align*}</span>  where no further forces act, <span class="math inline">\(f^\alpha_\gamma = 0\)</span>. For a point mass <span class="math inline">\(M\)</span> at the spatial origin, <span class="math inline">\(\left( \phi \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \right)(t, \xi) = - G_N M / |\xi|\)</span>, with <span class="math inline">\(|\xi| \coloneqq \sqrt{\textstyle\sum_\beta (\xi^\beta)^2}\)</span>, and this reduces to Newton’s law of universal gravitation,  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            m \, \ddot{\gamma}^\alpha_\mathcal{U}(t) = - \frac{G M m}{|\gamma_\mathcal{U}(t)|^3} \, \gamma^\alpha_\mathcal{U}(t),
            \qquad
            |\gamma_\mathcal{U}| \coloneqq \sqrt{\textstyle\sum_\beta \big( \gamma^\beta_\mathcal{U} \big)^2}.
        \end{align*}</span>  Gravity thus moves from the forces into the connection. Note that, in other stratified charts, <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma^\alpha_{00}\)</span> mixes gravity with pseudo-forces, which only the curvature separates.</p></li>
<li><p>Gravity occupies the same slot, <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma^\alpha_{00}\)</span>, as the translational pseudo-force, which raises the question whether it is a pseudo-force too. The answer depends on whether the gravitational field is uniform.</p>
<ol class="dg-enumerate dg-depth-1">
<li><p><em>Uniform gravity is a pseudo-force.</em> If <span class="math inline">\(\partial x_\alpha\left\lfloor \phi \right\rceil\)</span> is the same at every point, the chart <span class="math inline">\((\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y})\)</span> with <span class="math inline">\(\xi^\alpha = \eta^\alpha + b^\alpha(t)\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\ddot{b}^\alpha = - \partial x_\alpha\left\lfloor \phi \right\rceil\)</span>, whose origin falls freely, has <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma^\alpha_{00} = \partial x_\alpha\left\lfloor \phi \right\rceil + \ddot{b}^\alpha = 0\)</span>: in a freely falling elevator, uniform gravity disappears completely.</p></li>
<li><p><em>Non-uniform gravity is not.</em> The quadratic terms of the Riemann curvature vanish, since <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma^r_{jm} \neq 0\)</span> requires <span class="math inline">\(r\)</span> spatial and then <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma^i_{rk} = 0\)</span>, and its only non-vanishing component functions are  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
                    \mathrm{Riem}^\alpha_{0\beta0} = - \mathrm{Riem}^\alpha_{00\beta}
                    = \partial x_\beta\left\lfloor \partial x_\alpha\left\lfloor \phi \right\rceil \right\rceil.
                \end{align*}</span>  Wherever the gravitational field varies from point to point, <span class="math inline">\(\mathrm{Riem} \neq 0\)</span> in this chart, hence in every chart, and no choice of chart removes it.</p></li>
</ol></li>
<li><p>Spacetime, not space, is curved: <span class="math inline">\(\mathrm{Riem}^\alpha_{\beta\delta\kappa} = 0\)</span>, while every non-vanishing component carries the time index twice.</p></li>
</ul>
```

## `<span class="dg-secnum">9.5.1</span> Field Equation`{=html} {#subsection_Field_Equation}

```{=html}
<ul class="dg-itemize dg-depth-1">
<li><p>Poisson’s equation, which determines <span class="math inline">\(\phi\)</span> from <span class="math inline">\(\rho\)</span>, can be written in terms of the connection. The only non-vanishing component function of the Ricci curvature is <span class="math inline">\(\mathrm{Ric}_{00} = \mathrm{Riem}^\alpha_{0\alpha0} = \Delta \phi = 4 \pi G_N \rho\)</span>, and in a stratified chart <span class="math inline">\(dt\left\lceil \partial x_i \right\rfloor = \delta^0_i\)</span>. Both facts combine into the chart-independent statement  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            \mathrm{Ric}(\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y}) = 4 \pi G_N \rho \; dt\left\lceil \mathcal{X} \right\rfloor \, dt\left\lceil \mathcal{Y} \right\rfloor,
            \qquad \forall \, \mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y} \in \Gamma T\mathcal{M},
        \end{align*}</span>  which, both sides being <span class="math inline">\(C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\)</span>-bilinear, holds in every chart once verified in one.</p></li>
<li><p>Matter determines the Ricci curvature, and the curvature determines free fall: this is the time-time component of the Einstein equations.</p></li>
</ul>
```

## `<span class="dg-secnum">9.5.2</span> Tidal Acceleration`{=html} {#subsection_Tidal_Acceleration}

```{=html}
<ul class="dg-itemize dg-depth-1">
<li><p>Although non-uniform gravity cannot be removed globally, it can be removed along a single worldline, which is the content of the equivalence principle. Let <span class="math inline">\(\Phi \coloneqq \phi \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1}\)</span>, a function of <span class="math inline">\(\xi\)</span>, and consider again the chart <span class="math inline">\(\xi^\alpha = \eta^\alpha + b^\alpha(t)\)</span>, now with an origin falling freely in the non-uniform field, <span class="math inline">\(\ddot{b}^\alpha(t) = - \partial_\alpha \Phi\big( t, b(t) \big)\)</span>. Expanding around the origin,  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            \left( \Gamma_\mathscr{Y} \right)^\alpha_{00}(t, \eta)
            = \partial_\alpha \Phi\big( t, \eta + b(t) \big) + \ddot{b}^\alpha(t)
            = \partial_\beta \partial_\alpha \Phi\big( t, b(t) \big) \, \eta^\beta + \mathcal{O}\big( |\eta|^2 \big),
        \end{align*}</span>  which vanishes at the origin, <span class="math inline">\(\eta = 0\)</span>: an observer falling with it feels no gravity.</p></li>
<li><p>For a second freely falling particle, with spatial coordinates <span class="math inline">\(\gamma^\alpha_\mathcal{V}\)</span>, Newton I gives  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            \ddot{\gamma}^\alpha_\mathcal{V} = - \mathrm{Riem}^\alpha_{0\beta0} \, \gamma^\beta_\mathcal{V} + \mathcal{O}\big( |\gamma_\mathcal{V}|^2 \big),
        \end{align*}</span>  with <span class="math inline">\(\mathrm{Riem}^\alpha_{0\beta0} = \partial_\beta \partial_\alpha \Phi\big( t, b(t) \big)\)</span> evaluated at the origin. What survives in the falling chart is the relative acceleration of neighbouring free particles, the <strong>tidal acceleration</strong>, determined by the Riemann curvature: the part of gravity that cannot be transformed away.</p></li>
</ul>
```
